messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Park Ranger
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 41

He is 32, a North American man who works as a park ranger, and he describes his life as having divided into “before” and “after” a night that still feels unreal to him. Before the trauma, he is someone who knows the woods by sound and smell, who takes pride in being calm in emergencies and in moving quietly through remote terrain. He likes the solitude of the job, the long stretches of routine, the sense that he is useful without needing to be the center of anything. He is single, keeps to himself, and has built a life around predictability: early mornings, careful packing, checking radio batteries twice, drinking the same coffee before heading out.

The trauma happens while he is working in a remote area near the park boundary, where he is taken by men who accuse him of cooperating with authorities. He is restrained, moved from place to place, and held for what he experiences as an endless stretch of time. He does not speak much about the details, and when he does, his voice goes flat, as though he is reporting on someone else’s life. What stays with him is the helplessness: the inability to predict when pain will come, the way his body learns to brace before anything happens, the humiliation of being at the mercy of others. He remembers the sound of footsteps outside a door, the smell of damp concrete, the harshness of light when it is turned on suddenly. Even now, he seems to organize the event around fragments like these because the full memory feels too large to hold at once.

After he is released, he initially tells himself that he will recover if he simply gets back to work. He returns to the park as soon as he can, believing that being on familiar trails will help him feel like himself again. At first, the routine does provide some structure, but he notices that his body reacts before his mind does. The crack of a branch makes him jerk. When a hiker approaches too quickly from behind, he spins around with his heart pounding, embarrassed by how exposed he feels. He starts choosing routes with fewer people, preferring open areas where he can see what is coming. In the field, he is competent and outwardly steady, but he is constantly scanning. He keeps his back to walls, notices vehicles slowing near the trailhead, and feels a surge of dread when the radio crackles unexpectedly.

At night, sleep becomes difficult. He lies awake replaying pieces of the ordeal, not in order, but in flashes that arrive without warning. Sometimes he wakes from dreams with his jaw clenched and his fists tight against the sheets. He cannot always remember the dream, only the feeling that he has been caught somewhere inescapable. Mornings are often worse because he wakes already tense, as if he has been holding his breath all night. He drinks too much coffee and then feels more restless. On some days he feels strangely detached, moving through work tasks automatically while sensing that the world is slightly unreal, as though there is a pane of glass between him and everything around him.

He does not talk much to coworkers. He says he is “fine,” but he also notices that he has become more irritable and more easily startled, and he dislikes how quickly anger rises in him over small things. If a visitor ignores safety instructions or if someone jokes too loudly near him, he feels a flash of heat that surprises him. He has stopped going to the gym after work and no longer accepts invitations for drinks. He tells himself he prefers being alone, yet he also recognizes that isolation has become a kind of protection. He avoids news stories about kidnappings or political violence. He avoids certain roads, certain scents, certain kinds of rope or plastic ties in equipment lockers because they can bring the whole memory rushing back with a force that leaves him shaky and ashamed.

What he grieves most is the loss of ease in his own body. He misses the version of himself who could walk the backcountry without feeling watched, who could sleep deeply after a long shift, who did not need to measure every sound in the dark. He still loves the park, but even there he feels changed by what happened. The forest that once felt like home now sometimes feels too quiet, the silence carrying a threat he cannot name. Yet he keeps showing up. He checks the gates, greets hikers, and follows the seasonal rhythms of the work, even as he carries the experience with him in a way that is never far from the surface.
